GASTROINTESTINAL__Jaundice:
Jaundice is yellow discolouration of the sclera and skin from a raised bilirubin (clinically visible above ~40 µmol/L). Split it three ways: pre-hepatic (unconjugated — haemolysis, Gilbert’s), hepatic (hepatocellular — hepatitis, alcohol, drugs, cirrhosis) and post-hepatic (conjugated / obstructive — stones, tumour, PBC / PSC). Three clues localise it: urine (dark → conjugated), stool (pale → obstruction), itch (cholestasis), plus the LFT pattern (↑ALT / AST = hepatocellular; ↑ALP / GGT = cholestatic). Then screen the red flags (cholangitis, acute liver failure, painless malignant obstruction).
🚨Fever + right-upper-quadrant pain + jaundice (Charcot’s triad) is ascending cholangitis — a biliary-sepsis emergency needing antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP); add confusion and shock and it is Reynolds’ pentad. Jaundice with encephalopathy and coagulopathy is acute liver failure (think paracetamol — give NAC). Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier’s law) is pancreatic / biliary cancer until proven otherwise.

1Characterise & localise
🔍Characterise it
  • Bilirubin type: unconjugated (pre-hepatic) vs conjugated (hepatic / obstructive)
  • Urine & stool: dark urine + pale stool + itch → obstruction (conjugated); normal urine / stool → pre-hepatic
  • LFT pattern: ↑ALT / AST → hepatocellular; ↑ALP / GGT → cholestatic; plus pain, fever, weight loss
🚩Red flags
  • Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice (Charcot’s triad) → ascending cholangitis — antibiotics + urgent ERCP (see cholangitis)
  • Jaundice + encephalopathy + coagulopathy → acute liver failure (paracetamol → NAC; see acute liver failure)
  • Painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) → pancreatic / biliary cancer (see pancreatic cancer)
🩸Pre-hepatic (unconjugated)
  • Haemolysis: ↑unconjugated bilirubin, ↑LDH, ↑reticulocytes, ↓haptoglobin, a blood film (see anaemia)
  • Gilbert’s syndrome: a benign isolated unconjugated rise on fasting / illness, with otherwise normal LFTs
  • Normal urine and stool (no conjugated bilirubin to excrete); no itch
🫀Hepatic (hepatocellular)
  • Viral hepatitis (see viral hepatitis), alcoholic hepatitis (AST>ALT; see alcohol)
  • Drug-induced (paracetamol) (see DILI), autoimmune hepatitis
  • Cirrhosis (see cirrhosis) and HCC (see HCC) — ↑ALT / AST, look for stigmata of chronic liver disease
🚧Post-hepatic (obstructive)
  • Dark urine, pale stool, pruritus; ↑ALP / GGT and conjugated bilirubin
  • Common bile duct stone (see gallstones), pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma (see cholangiocarcinoma)
  • PBC (middle-aged woman, AMA; see PBC) and PSC (UC, beaded ducts; see PSC)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • LFTs with split bilirubin (conjugated vs unconjugated) and the ALT-vs-ALP pattern; clotting / albumin (synthetic function)
  • FBC, blood film, reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin (haemolysis); viral serology and autoantibodies (AMA, ASMA)
  • Ultrasound first-line (dilated ducts → obstruction) → MRCP / CT, then ERCP (therapeutic)
Localise with bilirubin type + urine / stool + the LFT pattern: unconjugated with normal urine → pre-hepatic (haemolysis / Gilbert’s); ↑ALT / AST → hepatocellular; dark urine + pale stool + itch + ↑ALP → obstruction. Ultrasound is the pivotal test — dilated ducts mean obstruction.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Groin Lump:
A groin lump is worked up by two questions: is it a hernia? and where is it relative to the pubic tubercle? An inguinal hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle; a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to it. Then read the character: a cough impulse and reducibility (hernia), pulsatile & expansile (femoral artery aneurysm), disappears on lying with a thrill (saphena varix), or it transilluminates (fluid). Screen the red flag: a tender, irreducible lump with no cough impulse is a strangulated hernia.
🚨A tender, irreducible groin lump with no cough impulse — especially with pain, vomiting or bowel obstruction — is a strangulated hernia (a surgical emergency: resuscitate, nil by mouth, urgent repair). Femoral hernias (commoner in women) have a high risk of strangulation and should be repaired promptly. Do not mistake a pulsatile, expansile lump (a femoral artery aneurysm) for a hernia.

1Characterise & localise
🔍Characterise it
  • Location vs the pubic tubercle: above & medial → inguinal; below & lateral → femoral
  • Cough impulse & reducibility (hernia); pulsatile & expansile (aneurysm); disappears on lying (saphena varix); transilluminates (fluid)
  • Examine standing and lying, check the scrotum (empty → undescended testis) and abdomen, and auscultate (bowel sounds in a hernia)
🚩Red flags
  • Tender, irreducible, no cough impulse (± vomiting / obstruction) → strangulated hernia — a surgical emergency (see hernias)
  • Femoral hernia (below & lateral, commoner in women) → high strangulation risk, repair promptly
  • Pulsatile, expansile lump → a femoral artery aneurysm — do not incise as a ‘hernia’
🕳️Hernias
  • Inguinal (commonest): above & medial to the pubic tubercle — indirect (through the deep ring, may reach the scrotum) or direct (through the posterior wall)
  • Femoral: below & lateral to the pubic tubercle — commoner in women, higher strangulation risk
  • Reducible (returns, cough impulse) vs irreducible / incarcerated; repair (see abdominal hernias)
🩸Vascular / venous
  • Femoral artery aneurysm: a pulsatile, expansile lump over the femoral artery
  • Saphena varix: a soft bluish lump at the saphenofemoral junction that disappears on lying, has a cough impulse / thrill, and comes with varicose veins
  • Femoral pseudoaneurysm: after femoral puncture / catheterisation (pulsatile, ± bruit)
🫘Nodes / testis / other
  • Inguinal lymphadenopathy: infection or malignancy — examine the drainage areas (leg, perineum, anal canal) and consider lymphoma
  • Undescended / ectopic testis: a groin lump with an empty scrotum (see scrotal lumps / testicular cancer)
  • Hydrocele of the cord, a lipoma, or a psoas abscess (fluctuant, ± hip / spine signs, TB)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine standing and lying: relation to the pubic tubercle, cough impulse, reducibility, pulsatility, transillumination, and the scrotum
  • Most hernias are a clinical diagnosis; use ultrasound for an uncertain lump, a vascular lesion or a node
  • CT for an occult hernia or a psoas abscess; node work-up (biopsy) if lymphadenopathy is unexplained
First decide hernia or not, then use the pubic tubercle: above & medial = inguinal, below & lateral = femoral. A cough impulse + reducibility means a hernia; pulsatile & expansile means an aneurysm; disappears on lying means a saphena varix. Tender + irreducible + no cough impulse = strangulation (operate).

GASTROINTESTINAL__Abdominal Distension:
Abdominal distension is a generalised swelling of the abdomen, classically worked through the six F’s: Fat (obesity), Fluid (ascites), Flatus (gas — obstruction / ileus), Faeces (constipation), Fetus (pregnancy) and a big organ or mass (organomegaly, tumour, a distended bladder; see Abdominal Mass). The examination pattern tells them apart: shifting dullness / a fluid thrill → fluid; resonant / tympanic → gas; you can’t get below it → pregnancy / bladder / pelvic. Then screen the red flags (obstruction, SBP, malignant ascites, perforation).
🚨Distension with colicky pain, vomiting and absolute constipation (no flatus) is bowel obstruction — make the patient nil by mouth, pass an NG tube and give IV fluids (“drip and suck”) and get surgical review. In known ascites, fever, abdominal pain or encephalopathy is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until a tap excludes it. New ascites with weight loss → suspect malignancy; distension with peritonism / rigidity → a perforation.

Always do a β-hCG in a woman of childbearing age, and never miss obstruction (colic + vomiting + absolute constipation).

GASTROINTESTINAL__Abdominal Mass:
An abdominal mass is worked up by two questions: where is it? (localise to a region — the nine regions) and what is its character? Ask the classic bedside questions: is it pulsatile & expansile (an aneurysm; see Pulsatile Abdominal Mass), does it move with respiration (liver, spleen, kidney), is it ballotable (renal), can you get above it (no → an upper-abdominal organ, e.g. liver / spleen), and can you get below it (no → it arises from the pelvis). Add consistency (hard / craggy → malignant) and tenderness. Region + character localises the organ; then screen the red flags (aneurysm, malignancy, sepsis).
🚨A central, pulsatile and expansile mass is an abdominal aortic aneurysm — if there is pain, tenderness or shock, treat as a rupture (urgent vascular review; do not delay for imaging in the unstable patient). A hard, craggy, fixed mass with weight loss or a hard left supraclavicular (Virchow’s) node is malignancy until proven otherwise. An acutely tender mass with fever / sepsis suggests an abscess, an appendix / diverticular phlegmon or obstruction.

🔍Characterise it
  • Region: localise to one of the nine regions — the organ beneath it drives the differential
  • Character: pulsatile & expansile → aneurysm; moves with respiration → liver / spleen / kidney; ballotable → renal; can’t get above it → upper-abdominal (liver / spleen); can’t get below it → arises from the pelvis
  • Consistency & tenderness: hard / craggy / fixed → malignant; tender + fever → inflammatory / abscess
🚩Red flags
  • Pulsatile, expansile central mass → AAA; with pain / tenderness / shock → treat as rupture (urgent)
  • Hard, craggy, fixed mass + weight loss or a Virchow’s node → malignancy
  • Tender mass + sepsis → abscess, appendix / diverticular phlegmon, or obstruction
🫀Upper abdomen
  • RUQ: hepatomegaly (moves with respiration, can’t get above it; see HCC / cirrhosis); a smooth gallbladder with painless jaundice (Courvoisier → pancreatic cancer)
  • Epigastric: gastric (see gastric cancer) or pancreatic mass / pseudocyst; a pulsatile AAA
  • LUQ: splenomegaly — moves with respiration, a notch, dull to percussion, not ballotable, you can’t get above it (see lymphoma)
🫘Flank / renal
  • Ballotable, bimanually palpable flank mass that moves with respiration
  • You can get above it, with a band of resonance (colon) over it — features of a renal mass
  • Causes: renal cell carcinoma (see RCC), hydronephrosis, polycystic kidneys (bilateral; see inherited kidney disease)
🩹Lower abdomen / pelvis
  • RIF: appendix mass (see appendicitis), caecal carcinoma (see colorectal cancer), Crohn’s (see IBD), TB, ovarian
  • LIF: diverticular mass (see diverticular disease), colorectal cancer, or loaded faeces
  • Suprapubic: bladder (retention — can’t get below it, dull; see urinary retention), uterus (fibroids / pregnancy; see fibroids), ovarian (see gynae cancer)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Run the bedside questions (get above it? ballotable? moves with respiration? pulsatile / expansile? bowel sounds or a bruit over it?); check for a hernia (see hernias) and lymph nodes
  • Bloods (FBC, U&E, LFTs, tumour markers as guided), urinalysis; a β-hCG in any woman of childbearing age
  • Ultrasound first-line; CT abdomen / pelvis to characterise and stage; urgent USS / CT for a suspected AAA
Two questions localise almost every mass: where is it (region → organ) and what is its character (pulsatile / expansile → aneurysm; moves with respiration → liver / spleen / kidney; ballotable → renal; can’t get below it → pelvic). Hard, craggy and fixed is malignant until proven otherwise, and a pulsatile expansile mass is an AAA until excluded.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Rectal Pain / Perianal:
Rectal / anal pain and a perianal lump are common anorectal presentations that are read at the bedside. Characterise the pain: severe tearing pain on defecation → fissure; constant throbbing pain with a hot swelling and fever → abscess; a sudden, acutely painful lump → a thrombosed external pile. Characterise the lump: position (clock-face), whether it is tender, reducible or discharging. Then split the acutely painful trio (abscess, thrombosed pile, fissure) from chronic lumps (prolapsing haemorrhoids, tags, fistula, prolapse) — and never miss perianal sepsis or an anal / rectal cancer. (For bleeding, see PR Bleeding.)
🚨A perianal abscess needs urgent surgical drainage (examination under anaesthesia) — antibiotics alone are not enough. In a diabetic or immunocompromised patient with pain out of proportion, crepitus, necrosis or systemic sepsis, think Fournier’s gangrene (necrotising fasciitis of the perineum — a surgical emergency: resuscitate, broad-spectrum antibiotics and immediate debridement). A hard, irregular, non-healing anal / rectal mass or ulcer with inguinal nodes (HPV / HIV risk) is anal / rectal cancer until proven otherwise — biopsy and refer on the suspected-cancer pathway.

1Characterise & localise
🔍Characterise it
  • Pain pattern: severe tearing pain on defecation → fissure; constant throbbing + hot swelling + fever → abscess; a sudden, acutely painful lump → thrombosed pile
  • Lump: position (clock-face), tender / hot, reducible vs irreducible, and any discharging opening (fistula / sinus)
  • Associated features: bleeding, pus / discharge, itch, prolapse, and systemic upset (fever → sepsis)
🚩Red flags & sepsis
  • Perianal abscess / sepsis → urgent EUA + incision & drainage (antibiotics alone will not cure it)
  • Fournier’s gangrene — diabetic / immunocompromised, pain out of proportion, crepitus or necrosis → surgical emergency
  • Anal / rectal cancer — a hard, irregular, non-healing mass or ulcer, inguinal nodes, HPV / HIV; biopsy and refer (2-week-wait)
🔥The acutely painful
  • Perianal abscess — constant throbbing pain, a hot tender fluctuant swelling, worse sitting, often febrile
  • Thrombosed external haemorrhoid (perianal haematoma) — a sudden, exquisitely tender blue / purple lump
  • Anal fissure — severe pain on defecation with bright red blood and a sentinel skin tag (posterior midline)
🍑Chronic lumps / prolapse
  • Haemorrhoids — a prolapsing lump with bright red bleeding (graded I–IV); usually painless unless thrombosed
  • Skin tags — painless, often after a fissure or haemorrhoid
  • Fistula-in-ano — a discharging perianal opening with recurrent abscesses; rectal prolapse — full-thickness protrusion (elderly women, children)
🧫Inflammatory / infective
  • Perianal Crohn’s — fistulae, abscesses, tags and multiple / lateral fissures with diarrhoea (see IBD)
  • Pilonidal disease — a natal-cleft sinus / abscess in a young, hairy man
  • Anogenital warts (HPV) and other STIs; proctitis and pruritus ani
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Inspection (clock-face), DRE and proctoscopy; EUA if too painful to examine awake
  • MRI pelvis for fistula tracks / complex sepsis; biopsy any suspicious mass or ulcer
  • Refer 2-week-wait for suspected cancer; HIV / STI screen for warts or anal cancer
Two questions triage it: is it acutely painful? (abscess, thrombosed pile, fissure) and is there sepsis or a mass? (drain the abscess / refer the cancer). Never treat a perianal abscess with antibiotics alone, and never dismiss a hard, non-healing anal ulcer — it is cancer until excluded.

GASTROINTESTINAL__PR Bleeding:
PR (rectal) bleeding is blood passed per rectum — usually a lower-GI source (distal to the ligament of Treitz), in contrast to melaena (black, tarry — an upper-GI bleed; see Vomiting Blood & Black Stools). Characterise it: colour (bright red = anorectal / distal; darker / plum = more proximal colon; maroon or brisk = a right-colon or a rapid upper bleed) and relation to stool (on the paper / coating the stool = outlet; mixed through the stool = colonic). Then work the differential by pattern, screen the red flags (colorectal cancer), and resuscitate the acute severe bleed.
🚨Do not blame haemorrhoids for rectal bleeding in an older patient without excluding colorectal cancer (change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, a mass, or age ≥50 with rectal bleeding → suspected-cancer pathway; see Change in Bowel Habit). Large-volume PR bleeding with shock → resuscitate (ABCDE, crossmatch, major haemorrhage protocol). And remember a brisk upper-GI bleed can present as red PR blood — do an OGD if unstable with no lower source. In anyone with a previous aortic-graft repair, a small ‘herald’ bleed then massive haemorrhage is an aorto-enteric fistula until proven otherwise.

🔍Characterise it
  • Colour: bright red → anorectal / distal; dark / plum → more proximal colon; maroon / brisk → right colon or a rapid upper bleed
  • Relation to stool: on the paper / coating / dripping → outlet (anorectal); mixed through the stool → colonic
  • Pain (painful → fissure) and associated features (mucus, tenesmus, change in bowel habit, weight loss)
🚩Red flags & the severe bleed
  • Change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia, a mass, or age ≥50 with rectal bleeding → colorectal-cancer pathway
  • Large-volume bleeding + haemodynamic instability → resuscitate (ABCDE, crossmatch, major haemorrhage protocol)
  • A brisk upper-GI bleed can mimic red PR blood — OGD if unstable with no lower source; never anchor on haemorrhoids in the older
🍑Anorectal / outlet (bright red)
  • Haemorrhoids — painless, bright red on the paper / coating the stool / dripping into the pan
  • Anal fissure — painful, bright red with a hard stool (posterior midline tear)
  • Proctitis and other anorectal disease (see anorectal disease)
🧫Colonic / structural
  • Colorectal cancer — blood mixed in, change in bowel habit, weight loss (the must-exclude)
  • Diverticular disease — a brisk, painless bleed (commonest cause of acute lower-GI haemorrhage)
  • Angiodysplasia (elderly, recurrent, painless) and polyps; ischaemic colitis
🔥Inflammatory / infective
  • Inflammatory bowel disease — bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency and pain, in a younger patient
  • Infective colitis (Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli O157, amoebic dysentery — see infective causes)
  • Radiation proctitis (previous pelvic radiotherapy)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • PR examination + proctoscopy (haemorrhoids, fissure, a low rectal mass); assess haemodynamics
  • Bloods: FBC, U&E, clotting, group & save / crossmatch; FIT and the 2-week-wait pathway if red flags
  • Colonoscopy (stable / elective); CT angiography for acute severe bleeding; OGD if an upper source is possible
Two moves triage it: where & what pattern? (bright red on the paper → anorectal / usually benign; blood mixed through the stool with systemic features → colonic / inflammatory) and is it severe? (shock → resuscitate). Rectal bleeding in the older patient is colorectal cancer until excluded — and a brisk upper-GI bleed can masquerade as red PR blood.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Steatorrhoea:
Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats and is hard to flush — the hallmark of fat malabsorption. Digesting fat needs three things: pancreatic lipase, bile (to emulsify it) and a healthy small-bowel mucosa (to absorb it) — so steatorrhoea localises to one of three buckets: pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, bile deficiency / cholestasis, or small-bowel / mucosal disease. Look for weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin (A, D, E, K) deficiency. Work it in three moves: recognise it, localise the mechanism, and investigate (faecal elastase, coeliac serology, imaging). See also Diarrhoea.
🚨Do not miss pancreatic cancer — steatorrhoea with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss (it blocks both the pancreatic duct and the bile duct; see Jaundice). Watch for fat-soluble vitamin deficiency: vitamin K → bleeding / raised INR, vitamin D → osteomalacia / hypocalcaemia, vitamin A → night blindness, vitamin E → neurological signs. New steatorrhoea with weight loss in an older patient needs prompt investigation.

1Recognise & localise
🔍Recognise it
  • Pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stool that floats and is difficult to flush (oil droplets / a film)
  • Usually with weight loss and features of malabsorption / nutritional deficiency
  • It is a malabsorptive diarrhoea — distinguish it from watery / bloody stool (see Change in Bowel Habit)
🚩Red flags & ADEK deficiency
  • Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss + steatorrhoea → pancreatic cancer until proven otherwise
  • Vitamin K → bruising / bleeding / raised INR; vitamin D → osteomalacia / hypocalcaemia
  • Vitamin A → night blindness; vitamin E → neuropathy / ataxia; plus progressive weight loss
🥩Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
  • Chronic pancreatitis (alcohol), pancreatic cancer, and cystic fibrosis
  • Loss of pancreatic lipase → fat maldigestion; a low faecal elastase confirms it
  • Treat with pancreatic enzyme replacement (PERT / Creon) and fat-soluble vitamins
🟡Bile deficiency / cholestasis
  • Obstructive jaundice (gallstones, pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, PBC / PSC) — pale stool + dark urine + jaundice
  • Without bile, fat is not emulsified → malabsorption
  • Also terminal-ileal disease / resection (Crohn’s) — bile acids are lost, not recycled
🌾Small-bowel / mucosal disease
  • Coeliac disease (villous atrophy), Crohn’s, and small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO)
  • The absorptive surface is damaged / bypassed — fat (and other nutrients) are not taken up
  • Also giardiasis, Whipple’s disease and short-bowel syndrome
🩺Assess & investigate
  • History (alcohol, pain, jaundice, weight loss, surgery), exam (jaundice, cachexia, CLD signs)
  • Faecal elastase (pancreatic), coeliac serology + duodenal biopsy, LFTs, USS / CT / MRCP
  • Check INR (vit K), calcium & vitamin D, A / E, B12 / folate; treat the cause & replace vitamins
Steatorrhoea = fat malabsorption. Localise it to one of three: the pancreas (low faecal elastase → enzyme replacement), the bile (jaundice + pale stool → relieve obstruction), or the small-bowel mucosa (coeliac serology / biopsy). And always replace the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) and check the INR.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Constipation:
Constipation is infrequent (<3 stools/week) or difficult defecation — hard or lumpy stool, straining, a sense of incomplete evacuation or blockage, and needing manual manoeuvres. It is extremely common and usually primary (functional), but you must exclude secondary causes (drugs, metabolic, mechanical, neurological) and screen the red flags — a new change in an older patient can be colorectal cancer. Work it in three moves: characterise, exclude secondary causes, and manage (lifestyle → the laxative ladder), treating any impaction. (See also Change in Bowel Habit.)
🚨Red flags: new constipation ≥60, PR bleeding, weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or an abdominal / rectal mass → suspect colorectal cancer. Acute constipation with distension, vomiting and no flatus → bowel obstruction (surgical). Constipation with back pain, urinary retention / incontinence and saddle anaesthesia → cauda equina syndrome (emergency MRI). And beware overflow diarrhoea from faecal impaction.

1Characterise & find the cause
🔍Define & characterise
  • <3 stools/week, hard / lumpy stool (Bristol 1–2), straining, incomplete evacuation, a sense of blockage, or manual manoeuvres
  • Ask about onset (acute vs chronic), stool frequency & consistency, and any red-flag features
  • Examine the abdomen and do a PR (impaction, mass, anal fissure, tone / sensation)
🚩Red flags & emergencies
  • New constipation ≥60, PR bleeding, weight loss, IDA or a mass → colorectal cancer — FIT / colonoscopy
  • Acute + distension + vomiting + no flatus → bowel obstruction (surgical)
  • Back pain + urinary retention / incontinence + saddle anaesthesia → cauda equina (emergency MRI); overflow diarrhoea = impaction
💊Drugs — the commonest secondary cause
  • Opioids (the classic culprit), iron, anticholinergics (antimuscarinics, TCAs, antipsychotics)
  • Calcium-channel blockers (verapamil), calcium / aluminium antacids, ondansetron
  • Always review the drug chart — and co-prescribe a laxative with opioids
⚗️Metabolic & endocrine
  • Hypercalcaemia, hypothyroidism, hypokalaemia
  • Diabetes (autonomic neuropathy) and pregnancy (progesterone slows the gut)
  • Dehydration and immobility — common and reversible contributors
🧠Mechanical & neurological
  • Colorectal cancer / stricture, bowel obstruction, diverticular stricture
  • Anal fissure / painful anorectal disease → withholding (see anorectal disease)
  • Parkinson’s, spinal cord / cauda equina lesions, MS, and Hirschsprung’s (from birth, in a child)
🪜Assess & the laxative ladder
  • Lifestyle first: more fibre, fluid, activity and good toileting habits
  • Ladder: bulk-forming (ispaghula) → osmotic (macrogol / lactulose) → stimulant (senna / bisacodyl) → softener / suppository / enema
  • Opioid-induced: osmotic + stimulant (avoid bulk-forming); consider a peripheral opioid antagonist (naloxegol)
Two questions carry it: is it primary or secondary? (review the drugs, and check calcium, thyroid and potassium) and are there red flags? (new change ≥60, PR bleeding, weight loss → cancer; distension + vomiting → obstruction). Most respond to fibre, fluid and the laxative ladder — and always co-prescribe a laxative with opioids.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Diarrhoea:
Diarrhoea is the passage of ≥3 loose or watery stools a day (or a persistent increase in looseness / frequency; >200 g/day). Two axes solve it. First, duration: acute (<2 weeks — usually infective and self-limiting) vs chronic (>4 weeks — needs a work-up, as for a change in bowel habit). Then, for chronic disease, the mechanism — secretory, osmotic, inflammatory or malabsorptive. The core skills are assessing dehydration & red flags, and knowing when (and when NOT) to investigate or give antibiotics — most acute diarrhoea is viral and needs only rehydration.
🚨Red flags: blood in the stool (dysentery, IBD, ischaemia), dehydration / shock / sepsis, recent antibiotics or hospital stay (C. difficile), immunocompromise, and severe pain with a distended abdomen (toxic megacolon). Chronic features (weight loss, nocturnal diarrhoea, >4–6 weeks) need investigation. Do not give loperamide or antibiotics in suspected E. coli O157 (haemolytic-uraemic syndrome risk) or C. difficile.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Change in Bowel Habit:
A change in bowel habit is a persistent change in the frequency, consistency or form of the stool — new looser / more frequent motions, or new constipation. It is a key finals presentation because it can be the first sign of colorectal cancer. Work it in three moves: characterise the change (what, how long, blood, weight loss), screen the red flags that trigger the suspected-cancer pathway (FIT & colonoscopy), and work the differential — structural (cancer, IBD, diverticular), functional / malabsorptive (IBS, coeliac) and systemic / drug causes. For the symptom-specific detail see Diarrhoea and Constipation.
🚨Screen for colorectal cancer: a persistent change to looser / more frequent stool (especially ≥60), rectal bleeding (see PR Bleeding), iron-deficiency anaemia, unexplained weight loss, or an abdominal / rectal mass → the suspected-cancer (2-week-wait) pathway, guided by a FIT test. Do not label a first presentation as IBS in an older patient or anyone with red flags. Also consider C. difficile after antibiotics and new inflammatory bowel disease. And remember a negative FIT does not exclude cancer — still refer with a mass, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia or persistent concern.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Vomiting Blood & Black:
Vomiting blood (haematemesis — fresh red if brisk, or ‘coffee-ground’ once altered by stomach acid) and black, tarry stools (melaena — digested blood, black, sticky and offensive) are the cardinal signs of an upper-GI bleed (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). Fresh red blood per rectum instead points to a lower-GI source (see PR Bleeding). It is a medical emergency: resuscitate first, then risk-score (Glasgow-Blatchford before endoscopy, Rockall after) and treat by cause — the decisive split is variceal vs non-variceal.
🚨Treat a significant bleed as a haemorrhage emergency: shock (tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria), ongoing haematemesis, or a large-volume bleed → ABCDE, two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch and the major haemorrhage protocol. A normal early haemoglobin does not exclude a big bleed (haemodilution lags). In known / suspected liver disease, assume varices and give terlipressin + antibiotics at once.

Painful swallowing (odynophagia) is pain on swallowing — distinct from difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), though the two often coexist. It points strongly to inflammation or ulceration of the swallowing tract. Two moves solve it: localise — oropharyngeal (a sore throat, pain at the start of the swallow) vs oesophageal (retrosternal pain a few seconds in) — and identify the cause, which is dominated by oesophagitis (infective, pill / chemical, or reflux). 🚨An airway emergency hides here: a patient who cannot swallow their own saliva (drooling), is febrile, with a muffled “hot-potato” voice or stridor may have epiglottitis, a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) or a deep-neck-space infection — get senior ENT / anaesthetic help and do not distress the airway (never examine the throat in suspected epiglottitis in a child). Also urgent: caustic ingestion, and progressive odynophagia with weight loss (oesophageal cancer).

GASTROINTESTINAL__Dysphagia:
Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) is a red-flag symptom until proven benign. Two questions solve it. First, where? — oropharyngeal (difficulty initiating the swallow, with coughing / choking, nasal regurgitation and a wet voice — usually neuromuscular) vs oesophageal (food sticks a few seconds after swallowing, felt retrosternally). Then, for oesophageal, what pattern? — mechanical (solids first, progressive → stricture / cancer / ring) vs motility (solids AND liquids from the start → achalasia / spasm / systemic sclerosis). 🚨Any new dysphagia needs urgent (2-week-wait) upper-GI endoscopy — especially progressive dysphagia to solids with weight loss, anaemia, or age ≥55 (exclude oesophageal / gastric cancer). And assess the swallow’s safety: coughing / choking, a wet voice or recurrent chest infections signal an unsafe swallow with aspiration risk → keep NBM and refer to SALT.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Heartburn & Acid Regur:
Heartburn (pyrosis — a retrosternal burning worse on lying, bending or after meals) and acid regurgitation (the effortless return of acid or food to the throat / mouth) are symptoms, not a diagnosis. Their commonest cause is gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), but they can be mimicked by cardiac pain and, when chronic, cause Barrett’s oesophagus and stricture. Work them in three moves: characterise the reflux symptoms (and spot the atypical / extra-oesophageal ones), screen the red flags, and step through the management ladder — lifestyle → antacid / alginate → PPI → (endoscopy) → surgery. (For epigastric pain / ulcer-type symptoms, see Dyspepsia.)
🚨Refer for urgent (2-week-wait) endoscopy if reflux is accompanied by dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 with weight loss plus reflux / dyspepsia; and for any GI bleed / iron-deficiency anaemia, persistent vomiting or an epigastric mass. And never assume “reflux” for chest pain until you have excluded a cardiac cause — reflux is a diagnosis of exclusion for chest pain (see Chest Pain).

1Characterise it
🔍Characterise the symptoms
  • Heartburn (pyrosis): retrosternal burning, worse lying flat / bending / after large meals, relieved by antacids
  • Acid regurgitation: effortless return of acid / food to the throat or mouth (no nausea or retching)
  • Waterbrash (sudden flood of saliva) and a sour taste; symptoms are often nocturnal
🚩Red flags & the cardiac mimic
  • Dysphagia (any age), weight loss, GI bleed / anaemia, persistent vomiting, an epigastric mass → urgent endoscopy
  • New reflux at age ≥55 with weight loss → 2-week-wait OGD (exclude oesophageal / gastric cancer — see Dysphagia)
  • Exclude cardiac chest pain — do not label exertional / radiating chest pain as reflux without an ECG
⚙️Mechanism & triggers
  • A weak / transiently relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter, often with a hiatus hernia
  • Raised intra-abdominal pressure — obesity, pregnancy, tight clothing, large meals
  • Triggers: fatty / spicy food, caffeine, chocolate, alcohol, smoking, late meals, and drugs (nitrates, CCBs, anticholinergics, theophylline, beta-agonists)
👂Atypical / extra-oesophageal
  • Chronic cough, nocturnal wheeze / asthma (see Asthma), hoarseness / laryngitis
  • Globus sensation, recurrent sore throat / sinusitis, and dental erosion
  • Non-cardiac chest pain — reflux is a common cause once the heart is excluded
⚠️Complications of chronic reflux
  • Reflux oesophagitis and peptic stricture (causing dysphagia)
  • Barrett’s oesophagus (columnar metaplasia) — premalignant, raising the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma
  • Aspiration, chronic anaemia, and dental damage
🪜The management ladder
  • Lifestyle: weight loss, smaller / earlier meals, stop smoking, cut alcohol / caffeine, raise the bed head
  • Antacids / alginates for symptom relief, then a full-dose PPI (4–8 weeks) — the mainstay
  • Refractory / red-flag → endoscopy and pH & manometry studies; then consider anti-reflux surgery (fundoplication)
Heartburn and regurgitation are symptoms; their commonest diagnosis is GORD. The test-of-treatment is simple: no red flags → lifestyle + a PPI trial, and a good response supports GORD. Red flags or a refractory / atypical picture → scope. And first, make sure the chest pain is not the heart.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Dyspepsia & Epigastric:
Dyspepsia (“indigestion”) is a symptom complex of epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness, early satiety, bloating and nausea. It is extremely common and usually benign (functional dyspepsia, GORD, peptic ulcer) — but a small number hide an upper-GI cancer. Work it in three moves: characterise the pain, screen the ALARM red flags that demand urgent endoscopy, and decide the pathway — H. pylori test-and-treat / a PPI trial versus a scope. And always exclude the cardiac, biliary and pancreatic mimics of epigastric pain (see also Abdominal Pain).
🚨Refer for urgent (2-week-wait) upper-GI endoscopy if there is dysphagia at any age, or age ≥55 with weight loss plus upper-abdominal pain / reflux / dyspepsia. The ALARMS red flags — Anaemia, Loss of weight, Anorexia, Recent onset / progressive, Melaena or haematemesis / epigastric mass, Swallowing difficulty — point to malignancy. And never forget the inferior MI that presents as “indigestion”.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Nausea & Vomiting:
Nausea & vomiting is one of the commonest presentations in medicine — and one of the most non-specific, because the vomiting centre in the medulla is driven from four directions: the chemoreceptor trigger zone (drugs, metabolic, toxins), the gut (vagal — obstruction, irritation), the vestibular system (motion, labyrinthitis) and higher centres (pain, smell, raised ICP). Work it in three moves: characterise the vomit (content, timing, force), split the cause into central vs peripheral, and triage the red flags & complications. Always keep bowel obstruction, raised ICP, DKA, inferior MI and, in any woman of reproductive age, pregnancy in mind.
🚨Do not miss: bilious or faeculent vomiting → bowel obstruction; haematemesis / coffee-ground → upper-GI bleed; projectile vomiting with a morning headache or focal neurology → raised intracranial pressure; projectile vomiting in a hungry 3–6-week infant → pyloric stenosis; and the systemic killers — DKA, inferior MI, Addisonian crisis and sepsis. Severe or protracted vomiting risks dehydration, hypokalaemia, a Mallory-Weiss tear or Boerhaave’s rupture.

  • Drugs / toxins: opioids, chemotherapy, digoxin, antibiotics, alcohol
  • Metabolic: DKA, uraemia, hypercalcaemia, hyponatraemia, Addisonian crisis

🩺Peripheral / GI causes
  • Gastroenteritis (commonest), bowel obstruction, gastric outlet obstruction / gastroparesis

  • Inferior MI and DKA — vomiting can be the presenting feature; ECG, glucose & ketones early

GASTROINTESTINAL__Peritonism (Guarding &:
Peritonism (peritonitis on examination) is the set of physical signs of an irritated parietal peritoneum — guarding, rigidity, rebound / percussion tenderness and pain worse on movement or coughing. It is the single most important thing to find in abdominal pain, because it separates a localised problem (an inflamed organ — appendicitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis) from generalised peritonitis (spillage / perforation) — a surgical acute abdomen. The key distinction is voluntary guarding (anticipatory, suppressible) versus involuntary guarding / rigidity (a reflex you cannot override), which is the hallmark of true peritonism.
🚨A board-like rigid, generally tender, silent abdomen in a shocked patient is generalised peritonitis until proven otherwise — from perforation, ischaemic bowel or spillage of pus / blood / bowel content. Resuscitate and call surgery now; do not wait for imaging. Remember peritoneal signs may be blunted in the elderly, immunosuppressed and pregnant.

1Recognise it
🔍What peritonism is
  • Signs of an inflamed parietal peritoneum — the sensitive lining that localises pain sharply and hurts on movement
  • Localised peritonism → a single inflamed organ (appendix, gallbladder, diverticulum); generalised → spillage / perforation
  • Distinct from visceral pain (dull, midline, poorly localised) — peritonism is sharp, localised and movement-sensitive
🚩Generalised peritonitis
  • Board-like rigidity, generalised tenderness, a silent (absent bowel sounds) abdomen and shock
  • Patient lies completely still — any movement, coughing or the car journey in hurt
  • Cause = perforation / ischaemia / spillage of pus, blood or bowel content → resuscitate & call surgery — see Acute Abdomen
✋Guarding & rigidity
  • Voluntary guarding: the patient tenses in anticipation — suppressible with distraction / gentle warm hands
  • Involuntary guarding: a reflex contraction the patient cannot override — this is true peritonism
  • Rigidity (“board-like”) is sustained involuntary guarding — the most extreme, ominous form
👇Rebound & percussion tenderness
  • Rebound tenderness: pain worse on sudden release of pressure (Blumberg’s sign) — but crude and unkind
  • Percussion tenderness & the cough test: gentler, more humane and equally reliable ways to show peritoneal irritation
  • Pain on coughing, moving or the bumps in the road is peritonism until proven otherwise — prefer these to hard rebound
🎯The special localising signs
  • Rovsing’s: pressing the LIF causes RIF pain → appendicitis; psoas / obturator signs → a retrocaecal / pelvic appendix
  • Murphy’s sign: RUQ pressure arrests inspiration → cholecystitis (localised biliary peritonism)
  • Cervical excitation & adnexal tenderness → pelvic peritonism (PID, ectopic) — do a βhCG
⚕️Confirm it is peritoneal — and act
  • Carnett’s test: tenderness that worsens on tensing the abdominal wall (head-lift) is wall, not peritoneum; if it eases, it is intra-abdominal
  • Generalised peritonism → resuscitate, NBM, IV, analgesia & call surgery; localised → target the organ
  • Do a PR / pelvic exam and, in women, a βhCG; peritoneal signs are muted in the elderly / immunosuppressed / pregnant
The question is always the same: is it localised or generalised? Localised peritonism points to one inflamed organ; generalised rigidity with shock means spillage / perforation — a surgical emergency. And it is involuntary guarding / rigidity, not the voluntary kind, that proves true peritoneal irritation.

GASTROINTESTINAL__Acute Abdomen:
An acute abdomen is the surgical-emergency subset of abdominal pain — a sudden, severe abdominal condition where the pivotal question is “does this abdomen need theatre?” Work it as a resus, not a work-up: recognise the surgical abdomen (peritonism — see Peritonism — and shock / sepsis), resuscitate in parallel (NBM, IV, fluids, analgesia, bloods incl. lactate & βhCG), then pattern the emergency (perforation, obstruction / strangulation, ischaemia, ruptured AAA, ruptured ectopic) and decide the pathway — theatre vs conservative.
🚨A rigid, silent abdomen in a shocked patient is a surgical emergency — resuscitate and call surgery now, do not wait for imaging. Do not miss perforation (free air), strangulated obstruction / mesenteric ischaemia (pain out of proportion, high lactate), a ruptured AAA (older, back / flank pain, shock, pulsatile mass) and a ruptured ectopic (reproductive-age woman — βhCG). And beware the medical mimics (inferior MI, DKA) — do not take these to theatre.

🔍Recognise a surgical abdomen
  • Sudden, severe pain in a patient who looks systemically unwell (tachycardic, hypotensive, febrile, oliguric)
  • The patient lies still (peritonitis — movement hurts) vs writhes / cannot settle (colic — obstruction, stone)
  • The pivotal question is not the exact diagnosis but “does this need theatre?” — recognise, resuscitate, refer
🚩Peritonitis — the cardinal signs
  • Rigidity (board-like, involuntary), guarding, rebound / percussion tenderness, pain on coughing / movement
  • Absent bowel sounds (ileus) with a still, tense abdomen → generalised peritonitis until proven otherwise
  • Localised → a walled-off inflamed organ (appendix, gallbladder, diverticulum); generalised → perforation / spillage — see Peritonism
💥Perforation
  • Sudden severe generalised pain, rigid silent abdomen, shock; commonest = perforated peptic ulcer
  • Erect CXR: free air under the diaphragm (absent in ~30%) — CT is more sensitive
  • Resuscitate, broad-spectrum antibiotics → theatre for washout & repair
🔄Obstruction & strangulation
  • Colicky central pain, distension, vomiting, absolute constipation; bowel sounds tinkling → then absent

  • Strangulation = obstruction + constant pain, tenderness, fever, tachycardia, high lactate → ischaemic bowel → theatre

  • Ruptured AAA: older, back / flank pain, shock, pulsatile expansile mass → theatre (do not delay for CT if unstable)

  • Basal pneumonia, Addisonian crisis, hypercalcaemia — a surgical-looking abdomen that a knife will not fix

GASTROINTESTINAL__Abdominal Pain:
Abdominal pain is one of medicine’s biggest presentations — spanning acute or chronic, benign or life-threatening, and surgical, medical or gynaecological causes. Work it up in three moves: characterise the pain (site, character, visceral vs parietal, colicky vs constant), localise it by region, and triage severity — a rigid, shocked abdomen is an Acute Abdomen (see also Peritonism).
